newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil anti-inflation plan completes third year.
newsitem.headline: Brazil anti-inflation plan completes third year.

text.p: Brazil on Tuesday marks the third anniversary of the Real Plan, a programme that has transformed the nation's economy from a hyper-inflated basket case into one of the world's hottest emerging markets.
The plan's cornerstone was the introduction of the real, a currency that has proved so stable that money counterfeiters are now back in business after years of hibernation under high inflation.
Backed by a strong currency and high interest rates, the Real Plan has wrestled annual inflation down from a dizzying 2,700 percent at its outset in July 1994 to about 8 percent today.

"There is still unfinished business in the plan, but I think we have done a good job. We have changed the face of this country," Gustavo Franco, a Central Bank director and one of the plan's architects, told Reuters in a recent interview.

For the first time in years, businesses and households can plan budgets beyond a few weeks. This has allowed millions of low-income Brazilians -- who never had an incentive to save -- to buy things like toasters and washing machines for the first time in their lives.
Government and independent studies also have shown that the poor are eating more meat, and for the first time in years accounting for a larger share of the national wealth.
That is one of the main reasons for the plan's enormous popularity. A poll last week found that 74 percent of Brazilians considered the Real Plan a success, while just 17 percent said it was bad.

The plan has also helped turn Brazil's image around in world markets. In early June, foreign investors gobbled up a $3.0 billion 30-year global bond offering, the largest ever offered by an emerging market country.

At home, stocks have soared 82 percent so far this year, surpassing yields on fixed-income funds, which have declined on a steady lowering of real interest rates from about 30 percent to 12 percent over the past two years.
But many economists say the market's exuberance is misplaced and is not warranted by the fundamentals.

On a recent visit to Sao Paulo, BankBoston Chief Economist Wayne Ayers said he was struck by the almost universal perception in Brazil that the progress made over the past three years was somehow irreversible.
"Frankly, it worries me," Ayers said.
While just about everyone agrees the plan has been a tremendous success, many are beginning to question how long it will be before deep cracks in the plan start to show.
Key constitutional reforms designed to solidify the Real Plan with sound fiscal and tax reform -- originally expected to be approved in 1995 -- are still sitting idle in Congress.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, the father of the Real Plan, already has an eye on next year's presidential election, which is set to replace reforms as the No. 1 item on his agenda.

Meanwhile, the nation's burgeoning trade deficit -- in large part caused by the strong real -- is pressuring the current account balance of payments gap, expected to hit $35 billion, or about 4.3 percent of Gross Domestic Product, this year.
To contain the rising gap, officials have been forced to limit economic growth, which posted a modest 2.91 percent last year.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor Rudiger Dornbusch, the most popular critic of the Real Plan, has long warned that Brazil will have to devalue the real by about 20 percent or face more serious problems down the road.
Now others are beginning to echo Dornbusch.

"We are worried about Brazil. If it posts annual growth of more than 3 percent, its balance of payments will unravel and problems will appear," Arturo Porzecanski, ING Barings chief economist for the Americas, said last week at a seminar in neighbouring Argentina.
Porzecanski said he expects a 15 percent devaluation of the real in early 1999 after the presidential election.

U.S. investment bank Bear Stearns entitled a recent report "Brazil: Much of the Good News is in." The report said the country was headed for its first major test since 1995, when it had to deal with fallout from the Mexican peso crisis and a consumption boom triggered by the Real Plan.
